title: Life without principle
hook: he warns against spending life only to earn a living (Life Without Principle)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the indifferent sea: Thoreau at the end of Cape Cod with all America behind him. Did a sky or a long view let you off the hook for a minute? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

Two men in the same woods. One walks there half of every day because he loves them. The other spends his whole day cutting them down for profit. Which one does the town respect? Thoreau poses almost exactly that question, and answers it himself: the walker gets called a loafer, and the man clearing the woods gets called industrious and enterprising. He isn't telling a joke. He's opening an essay about what a whole society rewards, and what it quietly calls a waste of time.
screen: `TWO MEN IN THE WOODS.` → `A LOAFER, AND AN ENTERPRISING CITIZEN.` → `WHAT DOES A TOWN REWARD?`

segments.voice: First, the bustle. The essay is called Life Without Principle, and one of its plainest lines is this: "This world is a place of business. What an infinite bustle!" Thoreau says he's woken at night by the noise of it. Trains, trading, hurry. Work in every direction, and almost no talk about why. Second, the loafer and the citizen. That's the story of the two men in the woods. His point isn't that work is bad. It's that we measure a life by what it earns, and so the person who loves the woods looks idle, and the one who strips them looks useful. Third, hire for love. He says, more or less, don't hire someone who does your work only for the money; hire the one who does it because they love it. Pay matters. But he says the aim of a worker should be to do a certain work well, not only to get a living from it. Fourth, more than a living. The heart of the essay is a worry: that we spend the whole of life getting a living, and never get around to living. Earning money isn't the enemy. Rent is real, and Thoreau took paid work himself, surveying land among other jobs. But he asks whether there's anything in your days that money didn't buy and couldn't. A walk. A friendship. A song you sing to nobody. It's an uncomfortable essay. It doesn't let anyone off easily, including its author. But the question at its center is simple enough to carry around: what in your life is more than a living?
screen: `A PLACE OF BUSINESS.` · `THE LOAFER AND THE CITIZEN.` · `HIRE FOR LOVE.` · then, large: `MORE THAN A LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing that isn't for money. Sit, and breathe. Let your work, paid or unpaid, settle at the edge of your mind for a moment. Then ask: what's one thing I could do today that earns nothing? Not as a reward, not to be more productive tomorrow. Just because it's good. A walk without a step count. A call to an old friend. Ten minutes with a book or a guitar or a garden. Let one thing come, and hold it. Picture yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
Life without principle. Thoreau's essay warning against spending the whole of life just getting a living. Today's word.
Your line: more than a living. Today, do the one thing you found, the one that earns nothing, and let it be enough. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of Life Without Principle take from it a habit of setting aside time for something done for love rather than pay, as a check on letting work fill the whole of life.
